name: redcon.c
baseline: Redis 6.0.6 (the README writes 'Redis 6.06'), single-threaded stock redis-server
workload: redis-benchmark -q -t set,get -r 1000000 -n 10000000 against the example Redis clone (example/clone.c, single-threaded, built on redcon.c and evio.c) and against stock Redis 6.0.6, pipeline depths 1 to 128, on one AWS c5.2xlarge.
claimed_speedup: SET at pipeline 128: 2,122,295 vs 990,307 req/s (2.14x, derived from page data); GET at pipeline 128: 2,230,151 vs 1,208,751 req/s (1.85x, derived from page data); SET at pipeline 16: 1,310,787 vs 765,284 req/s; parity at pipeline 1 (SET 114,554 vs 114,467 req/s, GET 114,602 vs 114,888); about 7% less memory (79.7 MB vs 84.8 MB).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. The README build line is 'cc *.c && ./a.out' with no -O flag; the benchmark commands are stated (redis-benchmark -q -t set,get -r 1000000 -n 10000000 -P 16 against ports 6379 and 6380, other depths varied) but how the Redis binary was built and configured (persistence, save points) is not.
hardware: AWS c5.2xlarge instance (Intel Xeon 3.6 GHz per the README; exact CPU model not named). Whether redis-benchmark ran on the same machine is not stated.
stars_or_usage: 58 stars; C port of the widely used tidwall/redcon Go library
tradeoffs: It is a framework for writing Redis-protocol servers, not a Redis replacement. The example clone supports only SET (EX/PX/NX/XX/KEEPTTL), GET, DEL, KEYS, PING, FLUSHDB, DBSIZE and QUIT, with no persistence, replication, other data types, ACLs, pub/sub or scripting. The README example stores keys as NUL-terminated C strings, so keys are not binary safe. Single-threaded by default; redcon_main_mt adds threads, and the clone's multithreaded build serializes access with one global rwlock. Event loop comes from tidwall/evio.c (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS/BSD). Dependencies (hashmap.c, match.c) are fetched with pkg.sh.
caveats: First-party README numbers only. The comparison is a minimal key-value server against full Redis, so the speedup mostly measures how much work each server skips (no command table with ACL checks, no client tracking or stats, no persistence or replication backlog), not a faster event loop for the same job. Parity at pipeline 1 shows the test is client or network bound there. Redis 6.0.6 was released in 2020 and later Redis versions were not tested. Build flags unstated ('cc *.c' has no -O), Redis persistence settings unstated (default RDB save points could fork during a 10M-request run), CPU model not named. README memory line says the clone used about 7% less memory (79.7 MB to 84.8 MB). A parser bug (negative bulk lengths) was fixed on 2026-06-29, after the numbers were taken. No independent measurement found (two searches); I opened the README, example/README.md, example/clone.c and redcon.c.

name: mrloop
baseline: unnamed epoll-based echo server (README row 'epoll'; neither libuv nor libev is named)
workload: TCP echo server (examples/echo_server.c on io_uring) driven by haraldh/rust_echo_bench, compared with an epoll echo server whose source is not in the repo; connection count, message length and duration are not stated.
claimed_speedup: Echo server: mrloop 288,169 vs epoll 191,011 responses/sec (1.51x, derived from page data). Same README, against Go's gnet echo server (gnet-io/gnet-benchmarks): mrloop 2,128,669 vs gnet 2,438,766 R/s, i.e. mrloop is slower (0.87x, derived from page data). Also lists the key-value store mrcache built on it: GET of 16B key 9.8m reads/s vs redis 2.7m vs memcached 400k.
compiler_and_flags: Library and examples built with gcc -O3 (Makefile, bld and examples/bld). Compiler version not stated; the epoll baseline's build flags are not stated.
hardware: Not stated (no CPU model, core count, kernel version or NIC/loopback note); README only requires Linux kernel 5.4.1+.
stars_or_usage: 48 stars; the author's mrcache key-value store is built on it
tradeoffs: Linux only (io_uring via liburing, kernel 5.4.1+ per README, while mrcache asks for 5.5 to 5.8). Callback API: the application supplies a per-connection buffer (the echo example allocates 64 KB per connection) and submits writes with mr_writev. Single event loop object; small library (mrloop.c, mrloop.h). The repo's todo file lists 'Add tests' and notes that completion-queue entries can drop on overflow without IORING_SETUP_CQ_NODROP.
caveats: First-party README numbers with no hardware, kernel, connection count or message size, and the epoll server being compared is not identified or included in the repo, so the 1.51x cannot be reproduced. The README's own gnet row shows mrloop slower than gnet, a Go event loop that uses epoll on Linux, so the io_uring-over-epoll advantage is workload dependent. The mrcache figures differ between READMEs (mrloop README 9.8m vs redis 2.7m; mrcache README 18.6m vs redis 2.5m), and they measure the application, not the loop. No independent measurement found (one search); the README, Makefile, bld files, todo and examples/echo_server.c were read. The last commit is 2024-04-13 (about 2.5 years old).

name: agensio
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (HttpArena nginx entry with a custom C handler module); HttpArena rows for h2o and Drogon also compared
workload: HttpArena public leaderboard profiles (gcannon, h2load, h2load-h3 load generators; best of several runs per profile): HTTP/1.1, h2, h2c, h3 and TLS rows serving the arena's baseline, JSON and static-file endpoints. agensio's arena handler module is compiled in, as is nginx's.
claimed_speedup: static-tls-1024: 1,191,970 vs nginx 720,869 req/s (1.65x, derived from page data). baseline-h2-1024: 14,210,433 vs 3,320,285 (4.3x, derived). baseline-h2c-1024: 14,782,707 vs 2,490,271 (5.9x, derived). json-h2c-1024: 4,567,724 vs 1,730,838. static-h2-1024: 1,420,432 vs 796,607. baseline-h3-64: 8,634,941 vs 4,849,624. static-h3-64: 745,030 vs 361,025. baseline-4096 (HTTP/1.1): 3,558,559 vs 3,284,513 (1.08x); json-tls-4096: 1,716,076 vs 1,313,755. limited-conn-4096: 2,577,049 vs nginx 2,626,297 (nginx 2% ahead). Memory on baseline-4096: 297MiB vs nginx 3.5GiB. Against zix (the Zig leader entry): baseline-h2c-256 15,185,367 vs 13,956,726 (1.09x), -1024 14,782,707 vs 14,569,901, -4096 13,627,524 vs 13,411,078, at 1648.6% vs 3999.4% CPU; but zix is ahead on baseline-4096 (4,442,329), json-h2c (6,821,589 vs 4,567,724) and pipelined (58,761,616 vs 4,958,241). Against h2o and Drogon: ahead of Drogon on baseline-4096 (3,558,559 vs 2,022,710), json-tls (1,716,076 vs 253,055), limited-conn (2,577,049 vs 1,694,883) but behind Drogon on pipelined (4,958,241 vs 7,801,404); behind h2o on baseline-4096 (3,641,609), baseline-h2-1024 (15,633,023) and limited-conn (2,651,569), ahead of h2o on static-h2-1024 (1,420,432 vs 341,251) and json-tls (1,716,076 vs 1,229,462).
compiler_and_flags: From frameworks/agensio/Dockerfile (agensio tag v0.1.0-alpha.23): debian:trixie with build-essential (GCC, version not pinned in the Dockerfile; the agensio CLAUDE.md names GCC 14.2 for Debian 13), cmake -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DAGENSIO_TESTS=OFF -DAGENSIO_NATIVE=ON -DAGENSIO_HTTPARENA=ON, which adds -march=native; hardening is on by default in CMakeLists (stack-protector-strong, _FORTIFY_SOURCE=2, -ftrivial-auto-var-init=zero), and CMake's Release default for GCC is -O3 -DNDEBUG (inferred). nginx entry: 1.31.4 built with --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG', quictls for TLS/QUIC, ngx_brotli, custom ngx_http_httparena_module.
hardware: HttpArena current.json: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX 64-Cores (128 threads), 251Gi RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-22-generic, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), CPU governor performance.
tradeoffs: Static-file, reverse-proxy and FastCGI (PHP) server on standalone Asio with its own HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (QUIC, needs OpenSSL 3.5) layers; one event loop per core and a lock-free in-memory file cache. No on-the-fly compression (serves pre-compressed .br/.gz twins), no directory listing, no rate limiting, no wildcard or DNS-01 certificates, no OCSP stapling, no HTTP/3 0-RTT; Linux only. Memory per idle HTTP/2 connection is 19 KB vs nginx 7.5 KB (agensio CLAUDE.md).
caveats: Pre-alpha (0.1.0-alpha, version 0.1.0-alpha.69 released the day before the last commit) and the README warns of unfound bugs, some possibly security bugs. The HttpArena entry was submitted by the project author and the committed numbers come from the alpha.23 build, while the repo has since moved on. In HttpArena the benchmark endpoints are a handler module compiled into each server, so the rows measure the server's request path on tiny canned responses, not real applications. On the h2 and h2c rows agensio, zix and h2o all land at 14-16M req/s while agensio uses 1.5-1.9k percent CPU against 3-4k for zix and h2o, so those rows look load-generator bound and the gap to zix and h2o is within noise; the CPU column is the better discriminator there, and nginx at 3.3M and 6400% CPU is clearly server bound. nginx's config has no open_file_cache and 65536 worker_connections across 64 workers, which probably explains its 3.5GiB memory and part of the static-TLS gap against agensio's in-memory file cache. agensio also loses to nginx on limited-conn, to h2o on baseline and baseline-h2, to zix on baseline-4096 and json-h2c, and to Drogon on pipelined. All servers here are typed 'infrastructure' (Drogon is 'flagship'). The agensio repo's own CLAUDE.md reports a CPU-per-request advantage over nginx on an M1 Pro and a Ryzen 9 9900X (for example HTTP 1 KB 1.9-2.0 us vs 3.0 us per request, one worker, wrk), but its raw result files are not in the repo; a few rows (10 MB streams, HTTPS 10 MB, HTTP 100 KB on macOS) favour nginx by the author's own table. Rows are the best of several runs per profile.
